- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.

## How loops and reductions call the library

The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:

- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.

These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.

## The curator's decisions on the library

- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).
- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.

## Designing a change

- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
- A `fail` without a static argument has the result type `Any`. Where it must have a type, write the static argument, as `strToInt` calls `fail[\ZZ32\]`.
- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
- In an api, declare each top-level function and each member of a trait or object at the header that the component gives it. A function's header is its name, its static parameters with their bounds, its modifiers, its `throws` clause, its parameters' modifiers and types, and its return type. A function's parameters' names and a `where` clause do not count, but each static parameter's name counts (ledger row 836). Give an object's value parameters the api's names, because they are its fields (`compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path"). In the cases below, change the component's header to the api's, not the api's to the component's. The examples are in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`.
  - The member's body already answers the api's type. `RR64`'s `opr |\self/|`, `opr |/self\|` and `truncate` answer `ZZ64`, because they call `Float`'s natives, which answer `ZZ64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:184-191`).
  - The api cannot name the component's type. `Array2`'s and `Array3`'s `bounds` and `zeroIndices` answered types of `RangeInternals`, which depends on this api. They now answer the api's `CompactFullRange` types, which those types extend.
  - The api's type is wider, and the overrides and bodies use only that type. `DelegatedIndexed`'s `generator` answers the api's `Generator[\E\]`, as `FlatString`'s override does.

  In the api, write `abstract` on each member that the component leaves without a body.
- The compiled checker's export check matches each api member with a component member of the same name and header. It matches these members in these ways:
  - A field, as `x: ZZ32` in an api's trait: by a component field of its name, its type and its modifiers other than `var`. A component's getter does not match it, so declare a field in the component too (ledger row 842).
  - An object's value parameter: by its type and its modifiers other than `var`, but not by its name.
  - A getter written `abstract`, as `abstract getter one(): T`: by a component getter at its header, or by a component field of its name and type that is neither `hidden` nor `private`. A `hidden` field has no getter.
  - Another member written `abstract`: by a component member at the api's header, with a body or without one.

  Each entry of the check's error names a trait or object and only its first member that differs. After you fix that member, check again to see the next. These steps run the check:
  - For a component of a compiled program or test: `fortress compile`.
  - For the one library's `FortressLibrary` component: the count stage (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time").
  - For the other thirteen components that the gate's distance stage checks: that stage. When a rung needs it, the brief gives its command.
  - For another component of the one library: no step, until the switch-over.
- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
- Write a new native as a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, and bind it with `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")`. Both paths run it. Give it the Java types that carry the declared types (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"). Write a glue class under `interpreter/glue/prim/`, which only walk runs, only where no Java type carries a declared type, as for `IntLiteral`'s bindings. Most of the library's bindings still name glue classes. A native is an edit of Java: rebuild (`build-and-caches.md`, "Two layers of code"), and test it on both paths (`compiler.md`, "Natives").
- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.

## Editing

A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.
# The Claude Code session: the Bash tool, long commands, waits and stops

**prompt cache**
: API's copy of a conversation's context. It lives five minutes for an agent and one hour for the main session. Each request to the API within that time reads the cache and renews it. The first request after a longer wait writes the whole context again: late in a long task, hundreds of thousands of tokens.

**interrupt**
: Stop of the session's turn, by the stop button. It kills every agent that runs in the background at that moment, of the Agent tool or of a Workflow.

**stop of the process**
: End of the session's Claude Code process. It kills every agent. It keeps the conversation, the transcripts and the disk: worktrees, uncommitted edits and logs. A command started with `nohup` (below) survives a stop, but not a restart of the machine.

**automatic permission check**
: Check that approves each tool call in auto mode. It can refuse a call, also a call that the curator approved in chat.

## The Bash tool and waits

The Bash tool stops a call at 120 s, unless the call passes a longer `timeout`, at most 600 s. It kills the command, or moves it to the background. It also refuses a command that starts with `sleep N` and goes on to another command, such as `sleep 60; tail build.log`. Wait with `wait_for` instead (below).

- In an agent, keep every wait under 270 s.
- In the main session, keep every wait under an hour. The main session can also watch a run with the `Monitor` tool.

## Long commands

If a command can take more than a minute or two, start it detached with `nohup`, after the setup lines, whose exports it inherits. Write the command and the log in the line itself:

    nohup bash -c '( ant compileAll ) > tmp/build.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/build.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &

Keep the setup lines and the `nohup` line as separate lines. `A && nohup B &` runs `A` in the background too, so its `cd` and its exports do not reach the lines after it in the same call.

The log gets the output, then a last line `EXIT=<status>`. The automatic permission check refuses a shell function that passes the command to `bash -c` in a variable, because it cannot read the command.

The shell function `wait_for` waits for the `EXIT=` line, for 270 s at most. If the line is there, it prints the log's verdict lines and returns 0: ant's `BUILD` and `Total time:`, JUnit's `OK (`, `FAILURES!!!` and `Tests run:`, and `EXIT=`. If not, it returns 1.

Run `wait_for` until it returns 0, each time in a new Bash call. Give that call a `timeout` above 270 s, such as 300000 ms. Define the function in each call that uses it. Grep the log for the lines that you need.

    wait_for () {    # wait_for <logfile> [max seconds, at most 270]; call again until it returns 0
        local n=0 max=${2:-270}
        case "$max" in ''|*[!0-9]*) max=270 ;; esac ; [ "$max" -gt 270 ] && max=270
        while ! grep -q '^EXIT=' "$1" 2>/dev/null ; do
            sleep 5 ; n=$((n+5))
            [ "$n" -ge "$max" ] && { echo "still running after ${n}s" ; return 1 ; }
        done
        grep -n '^BUILD \|^Total time:\|^OK (\|^FAILURES!!!\|^Tests run:\|^EXIT=' "$1"
    }

If your brief says that you run beside a batch, a run of other agents that build and test at the same time, run every build, suite, stage and program under `nice -n 19`, after `nohup`. Run one command of your own at a time that starts a JVM. The JVMs that it starts count with it.

- Start such a command only when the `available` column of `free -g` shows 6 GB or more. If it shows less, check again in each call of a wait, as `wait_for` waits, for at most 30 minutes. If it still shows less, start nothing and report back.
- A timed run of the checker is a plain run, under the rules for every other run here; it takes no lock and waits for no other work.

## Stopping processes

Stop only the processes that run under your tree's path. To find a process's path, read `readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd`, or the paths in its arguments.

Kill by process id, with `kill <pid>`. A pattern, as in `pkill -f`, also matches other agents' copies of the same scripts, and your own call's shell, which it then kills.

## After an interrupt or a stop of the process

If your work starts again after an interrupt or a stop of the process:

1. Read what is on disk first: `git log` and `git status` in your tree, and your logs.
2. If a step's log has ended and the tree has not changed since, the step is done. A log has ended if it has its `EXIT=` line, or its verdict or table is complete.
3. If a log has no `EXIT=` line yet, its command may still run. Look for its process under your tree's path. If it runs, wait for it with `wait_for`.
4. Continue at the first step whose log is missing, cut off or failed.

## When the automatic permission check refuses a call

- Do not try for the same result with another tool, by another route or in a later turn.
- Report the refusal and what was not done because of it. The way through is the curator's: manual approval for the session, or an allow rule for the command (`/permissions`).
# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:

         git push origin main
         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
         git push origin main:blinded-fable

     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.

# `widen` of a `ZZ` too large for 64 bits: the evidence

## 0. The question

`widen(self): ZZ64` on `trait ZZ` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:699`) converts the unbounded integer to the signed 64-bit one. For a value outside -2^63 to 2^63-1 there are two readings:

- keep the low 64 bits, as walk does today (row 502);
- raise `IntegerOverflow`, by the specification's general sentence on integer results (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:154-155`).

PLAN's natives line (`explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md:53`), PLAN item 31 (`:127`) and review-queue item 20 (`explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md:259-264`) hold the question with no default on record. The phase 3 exit judgement recommends the low 64 bits (section 4.3).

One citation to correct: PLAN's line, PLAN item 31 and the brief put "(row 349)" after the general sentence. Row 349 records that the compiler prelude's `trait ZZ` has neither `widen` nor `narrow`. The general sentence is cited by row 502 (section 4.1).

## 1. The specification

### 1.1 `widen` itself: not named

- No chapter of `Specification/` names `ZZ`'s `widen`. `grep -rnw widen Specification/` finds two other things only. One is a user function `widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\]`, the revival's example for the exclusion rule (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:433-443`, commit `3924e7ec3`). The other is the revival's Appendix I entry on the natives, which lists `ZZ32`'s `widen` among the 21 bindings moved onto helpers (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:4467-4472`). `ZZ32`'s `widen` is exact, so it raises the question nowhere.
- The Working Draft of February 2011 names no `widen` (`grep -rnw widen Specification-1.0-frozen/`: nothing). Its integer chapter has no fixed-size integer type at all: it lists `ZZ`, `ZZ*` and their refinements by sign (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:16-68`).
- The team's later restart has no `widen` either (`grep -rnw widen Documentation/`: nothing).
- Row 349's citation column and row 502's history give the same finding: "no prose chapter names `widen`" (`explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`, row 502).

### 1.2 Overflow: the general sentence and how far it reaches

The sentence, as the revised text has it:

    The handling of overflow depends on the type of the number produced.
    For integer results, overflow throws an \TYP{IntegerOverflow}.
    Rational computations do not overflow.

- Where it stands. It appears twice, in the subsections "Multiplication, Division, Modulo, and Remainder Operators" (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:113`, sentence at `:154-155`) and "Addition and Subtraction Operators" (`:190`, sentence at `:195-196`). Both are about operators. The Working Draft has it word for word at the same lines (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:154-155`, `:195-196`). So does the team's later restart (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Operators/operator-overview.tick:154-155`, `:195-196`).
- Wrapping has its own spelling. Each of the two subsections then says: "Wraparound addition and subtraction on fixed-size integers are expressed by ∔ and ∸. Saturating addition and subtraction ... by ⊞ and ⊟. These operations do not overflow." (`opr-overview.tex:205-209`; for multiplication, ⨰, and ⊡ or ⊠, `:172-176`). Both texts have these sentences.
- How far the revival has read it. The revised text applies "the rule for integer results above" to `GCD` and `LCM` (`opr-overview.tex:262-270`, callout `revival-gcd`). It also applies it to a `ZZ` shift too large to represent (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:738-739`) and to an integer power that is no integer (`:537`). P-73 reads it under walk as covering "every operation whose result can leave its type" (section 5).
- No passage applies it to a conversion, or exempts conversions from it.

### 1.3 Conversions between integer types, and `narrow`

The revised integer chapter, lines the revival wrote:

    An integer type coerces from each other integer type all of whose values it holds,
    as listed above; every other conversion between integer types is written explicitly.

    Among the explicit conversions, the method \VAR{narrow} converts a value of
    \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and a value of
    \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} to \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, by keeping its low 32 bits ...
    A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other wraps, and no
    \TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.

(`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:36-37`, `:39-45`.)

- The callout `revival-shifts` says: "The Working Draft of February 2011 named neither `narrow` nor `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT`, ... the two paragraphs above state the rules the revival decided for them" (`basic-integers.tex:63-66`).
- The Appendix I entry "Shifts and narrowing on the integer types" (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1723` onward) gives the reason. `narrow` "keeps the low 32 bits as the team's own test asserts at the values 2^64-1 and 2^63 (`ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss`, lines 210-211), on the signed types as on the unsigned" (`changes.tex:1760-1762`).
- So `ZZ`'s `narrow`, the sibling of `widen` in the same trait, is stated to wrap. `ZZ`'s `widen` is the one explicit conversion out of `ZZ` that the text leaves unstated. The rung that wrote the paragraph left it out on purpose: "`ZZ`'s `widen`, which walk also truncates to 64 bits (`BigNum.java:292-296`), is not stated: no decision covers it and its name promises no truncation; it is reported here and not chosen" (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-integer-rules/decision-record.md:42`).
- The coercion chapter's revision callout gives the revival's rule for the number types: "a conversion between number types is a coercion where it is exact and stays explicit where it can lose precision" (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:74-80`). It says which conversions are written out. It does not say what a written-out conversion does with a value that does not fit.

### 1.4 A conversion that the specification declares as throwing

- The binary-words chapter declares a conversion from a word to an integer with a `throws` clause: `signedIndex(): IndexInt throws { IntegerOverflow }` and `unsignedIndex(): IndexInt throws { IntegerOverflow }`. They are in `trait BasicBinaryOperations`, at `Specification/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1230-1231`, `:1292-1293` and `:1478-1479`. The Working Draft has them at the same lines.
- Their description is "[Description to be supplied.]", and the library does not build them.
- They are the specification's only conversion into an integer type that says what happens when the value does not fit, and what they say is `IntegerOverflow`.

### 1.5 Where the Working Draft differs

- The Working Draft has no fixed-size integer types in its integer chapter, and no `narrow`, `widen`, coercion between integer types or shift rule. All of section 1.3 is the revival's text.
- The general sentence (1.2) and the binary-words declarations (1.4) are the same in both texts.
- `IntegerOverflow` appears in the Working Draft only at the general sentence, the binary words and one method entry (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:777`).

## 2. The team's library and interpreter code

### 2.1 The declaration and its binding

- Api: `narrow(self): ZZ32` and `widen(self): ZZ64` on `trait ZZ` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:698-699`).
- Component, `trait ZZ` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:991` onward):

      narrow(self):ZZ32 =
          builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.BigNum$ToZZ32")
      (* This routine, named for consistency, converts to a ZZ64 *)
      widen(self):ZZ64 =
          builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.BigNum$ToZZ64")

  (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1080-1084`.) The comment is the team's, from 2009 (section 3).
- The two other `widen`s are exact. `ZZ32`'s binds the helper `simpleLongArith.intToLong` (`FortressLibrary.fss:805-806`, moved by climb batch 23). `ZZ64`'s is `widen(self):ZZ64 = self` (`:906`), which the revival added in `d846e3644` when `ZZ64` stopped being a subtype of `ZZ`. Before that, a `ZZ64` inherited `ZZ`'s `widen`.

### 2.2 The glue class behind `widen`

    public static final class ToZZ64 extends Z2L {
        protected long f(BigInteger x) {
            return x.longValue();
        }
    }

(`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/BigNum.java:292-296`.) Java's `BigInteger.longValue()` returns the low 64 bits. `ToZZ32` beside it is `x.intValue()` (`:286-290`), the low 32 bits. The revival has not changed either class (`git diff a874948ac` on the file touches neither).

### 2.3 The prelude's compiled helper: none

- The compiler prelude's `trait ZZ` declares no conversion out of `ZZ`: no `widen`, `narrow` or `asZZ64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:103-145`; row 349).
- `nativeHelpers/` has no `BigInteger`-to-`long` helper. `simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.java` holds the `ZZ` helpers: parse, print, arithmetic, comparisons, bit operations, `shiftLeft` and the conversions into `ZZ` (`:22-124`). The compiled `FZZ` class has no conversion to `long` either (`compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ.java`).
- The record classifies the binding as class C, "need a new helper" (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-23/probes/classified-base.tsv:115`: `FortressLibrary.fss 1083 ZZ widen widen(self):ZZ64 BigNum$ToZZ64 C`). PLAN gives class C to N3 (`PLAN.md:54`).
- PLAN's batch 24 is "N1's next families", the bindings that can already name a helper (`PLAN.md:46`). So whether batch 24 reaches `ZZ`'s `widen` is its planner's call. The planner's folder (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-24/`) names no `widen` yet.
- Whichever way is taken, the helper is new, and both paths will run it after the switch-over (P-58).
- A helper beside it already raises: `simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.shiftLeft` throws `Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$IntegerOverflow")` (`:93-102`). Walk turns such a raise into the library's own catchable `IntegerOverflow` (`interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java:184`; F-24).

### 2.4 The team's other narrowing conversions, at their last commit `a874948ac`

| Conversion | Path | Out of range | Source | Who, when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ZZ` to `ZZ64`, `widen` | walk | low 64 bits | `BigNum.java` `ToZZ64`, `x.longValue()` | Crink, 2009-09-10/11 (section 3) |
| `ZZ` to `ZZ32`, `narrow` | walk | low 32 bits | `BigNum.java` `ToZZ32`, `x.intValue()` | Crink, same commit |
| `ZZ64` to `ZZ32`, `narrow` | walk | run-ending error "Overflow of ZZ32" | `Long$FromLong` was `Int.rc(x)`; `Int.rc` calls `error("Overflow of ZZ32 " + i)` (`git show a874948ac:.../Int.java`, lines 239-245) | checked since at least the reorganisation `1d2680d4d` (jmaessen, 2008-03-24), where `narrow(a:ZZ64):ZZ32` bound `Int$FromLong`, which called `Int.rc` |
| `NN64` to `NN32`, `narrow` | walk | low 32 bits | `UnsignedLong$FromLong`, `(int) x`; asserted by `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss:210-211` | Steele (`gls`), `dc41d5000`, 2008-07-21 |
| `ZZ64` to `ZZ32`, `asZZ32` | compiled prelude | `IntegerOverflow` | `getter asZZ32(): ZZ32 = jLongOverflowingToInt(self)` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:581` now) | Steele, `9ce7d8189`, 2011-09-08, "New test Integer3 (has try-catch problems)": the commit changed `jLongToInt(self)` to `jLongOverflowingToInt(self)`, in the same diff that made `+`, `-`, `·`, `DIV`, negation and absolute value on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` checked |
| numeral to `ZZ64`, `asZZ64` | compiled run time | Java `Error` "Not in range for ZZ64" | `compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java:63-77` | team code at `a874948ac` |

- The compiler prelude's import block binds seven `long`-to-`int` natives: `longToInt`, `longOverflowingToInt`, `longLowHalfToInt`, `longHighHalfToInt`, `longMaskedToInt`, `longWrappingToInt` and `longSaturatingToInt`. At rung W's base (climb batch 2, 2026-09-20), past the import block, only the overflowing one was used for a conversion, by `asZZ32`, and the low-half one only for shift counts; the other five were used nowhere (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-int-conversions/REPORT.md`, "Precedent search").
- Rung W counted the convention of the prelude's integer traits: "thirty-two plainly-named members of the four numeric traits take an Overflowing native, and the wrapping and saturating spellings take the other two" (same report, "The specification, and the decision it does not make").
- The revival changed two of these rows. P-72 made walk's `ZZ64` `narrow` keep the low 32 bits (`d6faad28f`). It also added a wrapping `narrow` to the prelude (`d98024425`, then `ce0c7f453`, `CompilerBuiltin.fss:659`). The checked `asZZ32` stays.
- The one library's numeral conversions now refuse a numeral that does not fit. `IntLiteral$ToZZ64` throws `ProgramError` "Value ... does not fit in ZZ64" (`interpreter/glue/prim/IntLiteral.java:262-277`, `9d2e4c856`).

### 2.5 The library's own calls of `ZZ`'s `widen`

These are found by reading. Each call's argument is typed `ZZ`.

- `Library/QuickCheck.fss:322`, in `genZZ.perturb(obj: ZZ, ...)`, is `perturb(big(widen(obj) LSHIFT 32), ...)`, on the branch where `obj` is outside `ZZ32`.
  - The revival wrote this line in `d846e3644`, decision D10 of `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-flat-tower/REPORT.md:105`, "keeping the base's 64-bit behaviour". The team's line was `perturb(obj LSHIFT 32, ...)`.
  - Row 431 holds the bug: the line should shift right. Its fix, `perturb(obj RSHIFT 32, ...)`, removes this `widen`.
  - Measured, section 8.2: the gated team test `ProjectFortress/tests/ReflectiveQuickCheckTest.fss` reaches the line about 360 times a run. In two runs it never passed a value outside `ZZ64`.
- `Library/Format.fss:70`, in `radixHelper(base: ZZ64, val: ZZ64)`, is `n = widen(|/(val / base)\|)`.
  - `val / base` is a `QQ`, and `QQ`'s bracket answers `ZZ` (`FortressLibrary.fsi:437`). So the call is `ZZ`'s `widen`.
  - For any base of magnitude 2 or more, the quotient fits in `ZZ64`.
- `Library/Random.fss:203`, `random(): ZZ64 = widen(|\ asFloat(9007199254740992) __systemRandom() /|)`. Today the bracket on `RR64` answers `ZZ64` (`FortressLibrary.fsi:379`), so the `widen` is `ZZ64`'s identity.
  - P-68 makes the float brackets, `round` and `truncate` answer `ZZ` (row 330, one rung after the switch-over). From then on this call, and any program's `widen(⌊x⌋)` or `widen(round(x))`, goes through `ZZ`'s `widen`. This one stays below 2^53.
- No test in `ProjectFortress/` calls `widen` on a `ZZ`. Of the distinct `widen(...)` calls in its `.fss` files (`grep -rhoE 'widen\([^()]*(\([^()]*\))?[^()]*\)' ProjectFortress --include=*.fss | sort | uniq -c`), each argument is a numeral or a `ZZ32` or `NN32` value. The rung P skeptic's probe, `SkZZWiden.fss`, was removed in `ab067d9b6`.

## 3. What the team said later: the history

Method. `git log --full-history -S widen a874948ac` on each file. The conversion cut parent links, and the parentless full-tree snapshots it left were set aside (`research/authorship.md:14-22`). `-S` matches the substring, so hits on `widenUpper` and on the specification's `widens` were read and set aside.

| Commit | Date | Author | Message (verbatim) | What it did to `widen` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `1d2680d4d` | 2008-03-24 | jmaessen | "Massive library reorganization: ..." | Moved `widen(a:ZZ32):ZZ64` (glue `Long$ToLong`) and `narrow(a:ZZ64):ZZ32` (glue `Int$FromLong`, checked by `Int.rc`) into `Library/` |
| `29765a8e4` | 2008-03-28 | jmaessen | "Merged Thread into NativeSimpleTypes. ... Fiddled with some doc comments ..." | Added the doc comment "(** widen converts a ZZ32 into a valid ZZ64 quantity. **)" |
| `dc0f919ce` | 2008-05-08 | jmaessen | "Refactored libraries to move arithmetic operators from top level into the relevant traits and objects." | Moved `widen` into the traits |
| `fca589bbb` | 2008-07-15 | jmaessen | "IntLiteral is now a subtype of ZZ32 ..." | `widen(self):ZZ64` as a method of `ZZ32` |
| `e1567d62f` | 2009-09-10 | Crink | "Library, interpreter glue: Added methods to ZZ to convert to ZZ32 or ZZ64. The nomenclature needs work, in my opinion. Incidentally, my first ever use of Java." | Added `narrow` and `widen` on `ZZ`, the comment "This routine, named for consistency, converts to a ZZ64", and `BigNum$ToZZ32` and `ToZZ64` as `intValue()` and `longValue()` |
| `02e648434` | 2009-09-10 | Crink | "Reverting: Seems my r4150 was broken. Hmmmm. Seemed to test ok at work." | Removed them |
| `8d2eb48f5` | 2009-09-11 | Crink | "[library] Reinstating r4150; everything works now." | Put them back, the same 35 lines |

- At that time `ZZ` comprised `{ BigNum, ZZ64, NN64 }` (`8d2eb48f5`'s diff of `FortressLibrary.fsi`), so `ZZ64` and `NN64` values inherited `ZZ`'s `widen`.
- `research/authorship.md:68` leaves Crink unresolved: "editor support (GtkSourceView), library fixes 'tested at work'; likely external SCA contributor".
- From 2009-09-11 to the team's last commit, 2012-08-31, no commit changed `ZZ`'s `widen`. The search finds none, and since it is blind inside the parentless snapshots, the text was also compared: at `a874948ac` the declaration, its comment and `ToZZ64` read as `8d2eb48f5` left them (`git show a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, lines 886-889; `git show a874948ac:.../BigNum.java`, lines 270-274; `trait ZZ extends { Integral[\ZZ\] } comprises { BigNum, ZZ64, NN64 }` at line 533 of the api).

Their 12 hits are all on "widens", "widening" or "widenable", the widest-need evaluation of `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:835`, "Automatic Widening"; the last word is in `0f49d8698`, 2009-11-06, sukyoungryu: "components are widenable".

- Claim: "the compiler prelude's `trait ZZ` declares neither `widen` nor `narrow`, so `widen` of a `ZZ64` and `narrow` of a `ZZ`, which `walk` answers, are refused compiled; `narrow` of a `ZZ32` compiles by coercion and gives 43 on both paths."

The file has no `ZZ` value and no `widen` of a `ZZ`: its 15 `widen` calls take `NN32` values. So the judgement's reason is an analogy from `narrow` to `widen`.

### 4.4 PLAN and the review queue

- PLAN's natives line: "Asked: `widen` of a `ZZ` too large for `ZZ64` (row 502), which the natives meet when they bind `widen`: keep the low 64 bits, as walk does, or raise `IntegerOverflow` by the general sentence (row 349)? No default on record; the phase 3 exit judgement recommends the low 64 bits, before the natives bind `widen`" (`PLAN.md:53`). Item 31 is the same question (`:127`).

It notes: "that truncation is not a decision on record, only the tree's behaviour" (`explorations/reviews/wrap-dependent-code.md:20`). Of `narrow` it says: "The one integer decision that followed Java is `narrow`, which truncates as a Java cast does (row 346), and that is a conversion with its own name, not an arithmetic operator" (`:81`).

## 5. The record's decisions and facts

The record was read with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`, on every FACTS and POSITIONS entry that names `IntegerOverflow` or `widen`. Of those that name `ZZ64` or `ZZ`, the ones on numbers and conversions were read too. No entry decides `widen` of a `ZZ`. In POSITIONS, no entry names `widen`.

The decisions:

- **P-72**: "`narrow` keeps the low 32 bits of a value that the narrower type cannot hold, signed and unsigned, on both paths, and raises no `IntegerOverflow`."
  - It covers `ZZ64` to `ZZ32` and `NN64` to `NN32`, not `ZZ`. The audit says: "The entry omits unbounded `ZZ`" (`explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/full/evidence/P-72.md`, section 2).
  - Why, in its text: "the team's specification said nothing on `narrow`, and the team's boundary test ... asserts the low 32 bits for `NN64` values. On the unsigned types, keeping the low bits is a bit operation, like a shift, and the signed `narrow` gets the same answer."
  - Its origin: rung W (climb batch 2) had chosen the throw, under a silent specification and the prelude's convention (2.4). On 2026-09-22 the coordinator recommended "truncate on both paths, one prelude body, with the signed sibling checked to match. Rung W's choice on this point is reversed." The curator answered at 21:49:15Z: "Row 43 approved as recommended." On 2026-09-24 he extended it to the signed `narrow` (the same audit file, section 1).
  - The judgement of 2026-09-29 ruled on it: "a call following Steele's own 2008 boundary test ... against the general overflow sentence. Consistent with F2 and with what every JVM language does with a narrowing cast. Fine." (`explorations/reviews/decisions-review/judgement.md:146`).
- **P-73**: "Under walk, fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` when its result does not fit, on the unsigned `NN32` and `NN64` too. The rule covers every operation whose result can leave its type, `^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM` included." "Why: this is the specification's rule, and the compiled path already raised the error ..."
  - The curator's word was 2026-09-24T09:14:36Z, "Agreed with the recommendation." (`POSITIONS-history.md`, P-73).
- **P-70**: `LCM` raises `IntegerOverflow` when the multiple does not fit, and `GCD` where the divisor does not fit. "Why: ... its general rule raises `IntegerOverflow` for an integer result that does not fit."
- **P-153**: at a negative exponent, "the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`."

  - Under its rung, walk reads a `ZZ` exponent beyond 64 bits by its sign and parity, not by its low 64 bits. Its comment: "One beyond 64 bits becomes the long of its sign and parity nearest it" (`interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:268-283`; F-263, "including a `ZZ` exponent too large for 64 bits, such as 2^70").
  - The shift count follows the same idea: "The count is read by its value, whatever its type" (`basic-integers.tex:61-62`; P-69).
- **P-69**: on the fixed widths a shift "loses the bits that it shifts out, silently, as in every peer language"; on `ZZ`, `shift` is exact.
- **P-66**, the integer principle: "Java's and the JVM's defaults stay where they make sense, and are corrected where they fail high performance or mathematical precision. ... A hardware behaviour that bytecode can express gets its own explicit spelling, as the specification's wrapping and saturating operators do. ... The peers to compare are Julia, X10, Swift and Rust."
- **P-74**: "A conversion that is exact is implicit, and a conversion that can lose precision is written out." `widen` of a `ZZ` is written out. P-74 does not say what it does when it loses.
- **P-68**: the float brackets, `round` and `truncate` are to answer `ZZ`. This widens the reach of `ZZ`'s `widen` (2.5).
- **P-58**: every native binding becomes a `builtinPrimitive` call naming a static helper, which both paths run.
- **P-8**: where the designers' sources give no answer, the curator decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, "and he stays true to the spirit of Fortress".
- **P-26** and **P-27**, applied in order by the judgements: the type group's later positions over the specification's early text, then the library's own practice.

The facts:

- **F-132**: under walk, "Three kinds of operation raise nothing: the wrapping operators (F-130) and `narrow`, the written conversion of a `ZZ64` to `ZZ32` or an `NN64` to `NN32` (P-72), which keep the low bits; and the shifts `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT`, which lose the bits shifted out."
- **F-172**: "The specification's integer chapter states the library's integer rules. `narrow` converts a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` to `ZZ32`, and an `NN64` to `NN32`, by keeping the low 32 bits ..."
- **F-124**: on the compiled path `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits, "and `asZZ32` throws out of range".
- **F-24**: a helper's raise of `IntegerOverflow` is the library's catchable exception under walk.
- **F-130**: the wrapping operators, and `Random`'s `LinearCongruential`, which wraps through `widen` of its state. The library builds that object only at `ZZ64` (`Library/Random.fss:256-257`), so its `widen` is `ZZ64`'s identity, not `ZZ`'s.
- **F-263**: the power rules, with the `ZZ` exponent beyond 64 bits.
- The other entries that name `IntegerOverflow` (F-118, F-133, F-261, F-180) do not bear on conversions out of `ZZ`.

## 6. microGPT

- Neither program names `widen`, `ZZ`, `big`, `ZZ64`, `narrow`, `truncate`, `round` or a floor bracket. That was checked with `grep -nw` over `explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss` (98 lines) and `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss` (127 lines).
- The components they import beside them (`FlatArrays`, `FlatData`, `AplMg`, `AplMgSyntax`, `FlatArrays2`, `FlatData2`) name none of these either, outside one comment of `FlatArrays.fss` (line 6, "round three's survey"). Their one integer conversion from the library is `strToInt` (`FlatData.fss:34`, `FlatData2.fss:37`). It is `ZZ32` throughout (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4587-4603`).
- So, by reading, neither way changes a model line or the model's speed. Whether the library reaches `ZZ`'s `widen` inside a run of the model was not measured. Section 10 says how.

## 7. The peers

Each line was measured here, except where marked. Java is OpenJDK 25.0.4.1; Scala is the tree's `scala-library-2.13.18.jar`; Rust is rustc 1.97.0; Python is 3.13.16 with NumPy 2.5.3.

- **Java**: `BigInteger.longValue()` keeps the low 64 bits; `longValueExact()` throws `ArithmeticException`. The cast `(int) aLong` truncates; `Math.toIntExact` throws.
- **Scala**: `BigInt.toLong` keeps the low 64 bits. Scala has no checked conversion, only the test `isValidLong`.
- **Swift** (not run; read in `swiftlang/swift`, `stdlib/public/core/Integers.swift` on `main`, fetched 2026-10-31):
  - The plain conversion `Int64(x)` from any `BinaryInteger` traps: "If the value passed as `source` is not representable in this type, a runtime error may occur" (`:582-583`), and "Not enough bits to represent the passed value" (`:3427`).
  - The low bits are spelled `Int64(truncatingIfNeeded:)` (`:633`), saturation `Int64(clamping:)` (`:3136`), and the test `Int64(exactly:)`, which gives `nil`.
- **Rust**:
  - Primitives: `x as i64` from an `i128` keeps the low 64 bits; `i64::try_from` gives `Err(TryFromIntError(PosOverflow))`.
  - The standard library has no bignum. The `num-bigint` crate's `BigInt::to_i64` returns `Option<i64>`, `None` out of range, and its `TryFrom<&BigInt>` fails. It offers no truncating conversion (read in `rust-num/num-bigint`, `src/bigint/convert.rs:41-55`, `:107-132`, fetched 2026-10-31; not run).
- **Python**: `int` is unbounded and has no 64-bit type. At the places it narrows, `ctypes.c_int64(2**64+5).value` keeps the low bits (5). `struct.pack('<q', ...)`, `int.to_bytes(8, ..., signed=True)` and `numpy.int64(...)` raise (`struct.error`, `OverflowError`).
- **Julia**, which P-66 names (not run; by its documentation): `Int64(big(2)^64)` throws `InexactError`, and the low bits are spelled `x % Int64`. X10, which P-66 also names, was not checked.

content.content:
In short: Java's `longValue` and Scala's `toLong`, the plain methods of their bignums, keep the low bits, and Java also offers the checked `longValueExact`. Rust's `as` between primitive integers keeps the low bits too. Of the languages that P-66 names, Swift (read in its source) and Julia (by its documentation) make the plain conversion checked and spell the low bits separately, and Rust's bignum crate (read in its source) offers only checked conversions. Python has no 64-bit integer of its own, and its narrowing places split: `ctypes` keeps the low bits, `struct`, `to_bytes` and NumPy raise.

The commands, and the output that matters:

    $ jshell -q --class-path ProjectFortress/third_party/scala/scala-library-2.13.18.jar peers.jsh
    Java  BigInteger.longValue(2^64+5)      = 5
    Java  BigInteger.longValueExact(2^64+5) -> ArithmeticException: BigInteger out of long range
    Java  (int) 4294967301L                 = 5
    Java  Math.toIntExact(2^32+5)           -> ArithmeticException: integer overflow
    Scala BigInt(2^64+5).toLong             = 5
    Scala BigInt(2^64+5).isValidLong        = false

    $ rustc -O -o peers_rs peers.rs && ./peers_rs
    Rust  ((1i128<<64)+5) as i64       = 5
    Rust  i64::try_from((1i128<<64)+5) = Err(TryFromIntError(PosOverflow))

    $ python3 -I peers.py
    Python ctypes.c_int64(2**64+5).value = 5
    Python struct.pack('<q', 2**64+5) -> struct.error: 'q' format requires -9223372036854775808 <= number <= 9223372036854775807
    Python (2**64+5).to_bytes(8, signed=True) -> OverflowError: int too big to convert
    Python numpy.int64(2**64+5) -> OverflowError: Python int too large to convert to C long (numpy 2.5.3)

The three scripts are a few lines each: `BigInteger.TWO.pow(64).add(BigInteger.valueOf(5))` and `scala.math.BigInt.apply(z)` in jshell, `(1i128 << 64) + 5` in Rust, `2**64 + 5` in Python.

## 8. Runs under walk

The setup lines of the `fortress-repo` skill were used, with `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, and each run had a private caches folder (`FORTRESS_CACHES=<scratch>/caches`). The build was the tree's own, at `640acb4a1`.

### 8.1 The three-line program

    component WidenProbe
    export Executable
    run() = do
      println("widen(2^64 + 5)     = " widen(18446744073709551621))
      println("widen(-(2^63) - 1)  = " widen(-9223372036854775809))
      println("widen(2^63 - 1)     = " widen(big(9223372036854775807)))
    end
    end

Under walk the first two numerals do not fit `ZZ64`, so they are `ZZ` values (P-76), and `widen` runs `ZZ`'s binding. The third line is the control, a `ZZ` that fits.

    $ cd <scratch>/probe && FORTRESS_CACHES=<scratch>/caches bin/fortress WidenProbe.fss; echo "rc=$?"
    widen(2^64 + 5)     = 5
    widen(-(2^63) - 1)  = 9223372036854775807
    widen(2^63 - 1)     = 9223372036854775807
    rc=0

The run reproduces row 502: no error, the low 64 bits, and a negative input that comes out as the largest positive `ZZ64`.

### 8.2 Does a gated test pass `widen` a `ZZ` beyond 64 bits?

- The question is whether the raise would turn the team's QuickCheck test red through `QuickCheck.fss:322` (2.5).
- Method:
  - A copy of `Library/QuickCheck.fss` and `.fsi` went into a scratch folder. Walk's source path reads the current directory first (`fortress-repo`, `build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
  - Two lines were added to the copy's `genZZ.perturb`, on the branch that calls `widen`, which became a `do` block:

        println("PERTURB-ELSE " obj)
        if |obj| > big(9223372036854775807) then println("WIDEN-OUT-OF-RANGE " obj) end

  - `ProjectFortress/tests/ReflectiveQuickCheckTest.fss` was run twice from that folder, with its own private caches.
  - The cached tree of `QuickCheck` named the copy's path, so the copy was the one loaded.
- Result: run 1 had 356 `PERTURB-ELSE` lines and 0 `WIDEN-OUT-OF-RANGE`; run 2 had 370 and 0. Both runs passed all 9 properties and exited 0.
- The values that reached the call were within 64 bits, such as `-5105303812412827606`. They come from the line's own `widen(obj) LSHIFT 32` recursion.
- Two runs of a randomised test do not prove that a value beyond 64 bits never comes. `genZZ.generate` makes values beyond 2^64 at 4 of its 12 levels (`QuickCheck.fss:300-315`).

## 9. The ways

| Way | What it changes in the tree | What it costs | What it gives up |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Keep the low 64 bits** (walk today; the judgement's recommendation) | The binding at `FortressLibrary.fss:1083-1084` names a new helper in `simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.java` returning `x.longValue()`. A walk test asserts `widen(2^64+5) = 5` and `widen(-(2^63)-1) = 2^63-1`, and a compiled test binds the helper itself (as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` does). The specification gains a sentence on `widen` beside `narrow` (`basic-integers.tex:39-45`), with its callout and an Appendix I entry, and P-72 or a new entry records it. Row 502 closes as decided, and row 349's `widen` half at the switch-over. Walk's behaviour, the library's calls and microGPT do not change. | One helper of three lines and two tests, inside the natives family that moves the binding: 0 rungs of its own (judgement, 5.2). | A value too large becomes a wrong value with no signal, as row 502 shows: `-(2^63)-1` comes out as `2^63-1`. The general sentence (1.2) is not applied to this conversion. The plain-named narrowings of the type group's prelude (`asZZ32`, Steele 2011) and of the team's 2008 walk (`ZZ64`'s `narrow`) stay checked, and this one does not. The revival elsewhere reads a `ZZ` beyond 64 bits by its value (P-153's exponent, P-69's counts) and refuses a numeral that does not fit (2.4). Rung P wrote that the name "promises no truncation" (1.3). |
| **B. Raise `IntegerOverflow`** (the general sentence) | The binding names a new helper that throws `Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$IntegerOverflow")` when `x.bitLength() > 63`, else returns `x.longValue()`, in the form of `shiftLeft` beside it (2.3). Walk changes: row 502 is fixed by that commit, with a walk test using the `overflows(...)` form of `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss` and a compiled test of the helper. The specification sentence beside `narrow` says the conversion throws, with callout, Appendix I entry and a POSITIONS entry. `QuickCheck.fss:322` would raise for an `obj` beyond 64 bits; it was not reached in two runs (8.2), and row 431's fix removes the call. | The same helper and tests, plus one bit-length test per call; the run-time cost of that test was not measured. 0 rungs of its own. | Inside `trait ZZ`, `narrow` would keep the low 32 bits (stated, `basic-integers.tex:39-45`) while `widen` raised: the two conversions out of `ZZ` would differ. P-72's reason, keeping the low bits as a bit operation, would not extend to `widen`. No spelling would be left for "the low 64 bits of a `ZZ`": `trait ZZ` has no other conversion to a fixed width, so a program reduces the value into `ZZ64`'s range itself, with `MOD` or `BITAND` and a sign correction, before `widen`. The wrap review's device "`ZZ`'s `narrow` and `widen` keep the low bits" (`wrap-dependent-code.md:20`) loses its `widen` half. |
| **B′. Raise in both conversions out of `ZZ`** (`narrow` and `widen`) | As B, and `ZZ`'s `narrow` binds a raising helper too. The sentence `basic-integers.tex:39-45` and its Appendix I entry change for `ZZ`, which rung P's decision 4 stated (`decision-record.md:42`). P-72's entry is unchanged, since it omits `ZZ`. F-172 changes. | As B, plus a second helper and a reversed sentence of the specification. | As B, without the asymmetry inside `trait ZZ`. In its place, `ZZ`'s `narrow` would differ from `ZZ64`'s and `NN64`'s, which P-72 keeps wrapping. |
| **C. Raise, and spell the low bits separately** (Swift's `truncatingIfNeeded:`, Julia's `% Int64`; the prelude's reserved `Wrapping` and `Saturating` natives, 2.4) | As B, plus a new declaration on `ZZ` for the low 64 bits, with its own helper, test, specification sentence and name. | As B, plus one api member. Its name is new: a functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports the library (`fortress-repo`, `library.md`), and the name is the curator's. | As B, except that the low-bits spelling stays. It adds a member that the team's library never declared. |

Notes on the ways:

- **Which keeps the current behaviour.** Way A. Ways B, B′ and C change walk. None changes microGPT, by reading (6).
- **What none of them changes.** The compiled path has no `ZZ`'s `widen` until the switch-over (row 349). Whichever helper is written becomes the compiled answer then (P-58). The cost of a later reversal is one helper body, its test and the specification sentence.
- **When.**
  - The question must be answered before the binding at `FortressLibrary.fss:1083-1084` moves onto a helper, because the helper fixes the answer on both paths.
  - The record files that binding as class C, a new helper (2.3), which PLAN gives to N3. Whether climb batch 24 reaches it is its planner's call.
  - P-68's rung, after the switch-over, routes the float brackets, `round` and `truncate` through `ZZ` (2.5). From then on, `widen` of their results is the way a program gets a `ZZ64` from a float, and this choice decides what `widen(round(1.0e19))` does.

## 10. What is missing, and how to get it

- **Whether microGPT's run reaches `ZZ`'s `widen`.** Not measured. One way: count calls in a scratch copy of the library's `trait ZZ`, the method of 8.2, and run `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh` from that folder. By reading, neither program nor its components can reach it (6).
- **Swift, Rust's `num-bigint` and Julia were not run.** Swift and `num-bigint` were read in their sources, Julia from memory of its documentation. X10 was not checked.
- **The raising helper's cost per call.** Not measured. It is one `BigInteger.bitLength()` on a value that is already a `BigInteger`.
- **Whether `ReflectiveQuickCheckTest` ever passes a value beyond 64 bits to `QuickCheck.fss:322`.** Two runs passed none (8.2). More runs, or a seed sweep, would bound it further.

## 11. Findings new to the record

- `ZZ`'s `widen` and `narrow` are Crink's of 2009-09-10/11 (`e1567d62f`, reverted by `02e648434`, reinstated by `8d2eb48f5`). They were named "for consistency" with the exact `ZZ32` `widen`, "the nomenclature needs work", and left unchanged to `a874948ac` (section 3). No earlier record note names these commits.
- The prelude's checked `asZZ32` is Steele's change of `jLongToInt` to `jLongOverflowingToInt` in `9ce7d8189` (2011-09-08). It was made in the commit that made the prelude's plain arithmetic checked (section 2.4). The record cites that commit for the arithmetic (`wrap-dependent-code.md`), not for `asZZ32`.
- `ReflectiveQuickCheckTest` reaches `ZZ`'s `widen` at `QuickCheck.fss:322` about 360 times a run, with values within 64 bits in two runs (section 8.2).
- Two slips in the record's text of the question:
  - PLAN's natives line, PLAN item 31 and the brief cite row 349 for the general sentence, which row 502 cites (section 0).
  - Row 502's present class, `implementation gap (walk)`, presumes walk wrong while its notes leave the answer to the curator; its earlier class was "divergence, specification silent" (section 4.1).
- By the record's classification, `ZZ`'s `widen` is a class C binding, a new helper, which PLAN gives to N3, not to N1's next families (section 2.3).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:88
- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent. Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:56
- P-59 **Walk chooses a coercion by the run-time value until it runs the checker, after the switch-over.** Walk has no static types. So where a coercion is needed, walk chooses it by the value's run-time type. The specification and the compiled path choose it by the static type. The curator accepts this as the interpreter's limit, and walk is not changed for it before the switch-over. A callout in the coercion chapter (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`) states the limit. Two expected-failure tests record it: `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`, the chapter's own printed example, and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`. After the switch-over, once walk runs the checker on its programs (P-12 orders the two steps), it uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.

# Who wrote Fortress — an authorship map

Compiled 2026-08-21 from the git history (5,397 historical commits,
2007-01-04 → 2012-08-31) plus the 1.0 specification's acknowledgments,
the project's published papers, and public-web checks. Purpose: know who
wrote which subsystem, and whom one could plausibly contact with
questions about history or unrealized plans.

**Caveats.** The git record starts January 2007; the project began in 2003,
so four years of design history (and any pre-2007 code) predate every count
below — Eric Allen, for instance, was co-principal-investigator from the
start but shows only ~233 commits because the record starts late, and spec
co-authors **Sam Tobin-Hochstadt** and **Joe Hallett** have *zero* commits
here (their era's record is lost). Counts are `git log --full-history`
per path. Plain `git log -- <dir>` — and `git blame` — are broken in this
repository: the hg→git conversion behind the GitHub mirror
`sirinath/fortress`, of which this repository is a 2018 fork (see
`explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`), severed 146 parent links, turning
ordinary 2011–2012 java.net-era commits
into parentless full-tree snapshots, so any history walk from HEAD dead-ends
at the nearest phantom root instead of reaching 2007 (blame will credit an
entire untouched file to, e.g., a July 2012 seam commit). Those snapshot
roots also add up to ~146 spurious per-path "touched" credits inside the
`--full-history` counts — noise spread across 2011–12 committers, small at
the scale of the numbers above. In the other direction, the counts
*undercount* the 2008 research-branch authors: those branches were
svn-squash-merged into trunk, so the fine-grained per-commit record for
Culpepper, Rafkind, Lee, and Spiegel on that work survives only on the
relic branch heads, not in any walk from HEAD — see "The relic branches"
below. The
2007–2011 SVN/Mercurial history uses bare usernames (`sukyoungryu@localhost`
etc.); identities are resolved below with the evidence stated.

## The identity key

Three naming eras: Sun employee IDs (Jan–Jun 2007), SVN usernames
(June 2007 on), and real names (after the March 2011 move to Mercurial on
java.net). The ID→username handoffs are datable to days — each ID stops
committing within a week of its username starting, on the same files.

| Identity (commits, combined) | Usernames | Active | Who / evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sukyoung Ryu** (1,586) | sr155864, sukyoungryu, sukyoung | 2007-01 → 2011-09 | Certain — spec co-author; most prolific committer by far |
| **David Chase** (991) | dc12360, dr2chase, David Chase | 2007-01 → 2012-07 | Certain — spec co-author; `dr2chase` is his GitHub handle; owned the 2011 java.net migration |
| **Jan-Willem Maessen** (592) | jm143038, jmaessen | 2007-01 → 2010-03 | Certain — spec co-author |
| **Christine H. Flood** (261) | chf, chmf | 2007-01 → 2012-05 | **Verified**: her own bio — PLRG work on "the bytecode optimizer, software transactional memory, and compilation to a fork/join framework" — matches her commits exactly |
| **Justin Hilburn** (261) | jrhil47 | 2008-05 → 2011-09 | High — OOPSLA 2011 co-author; commits are overloading/OverloadingOracle, the paper's subject |
| **Jon Rafkind** (237) | jon | 2008-05 → 2009-08 | High — all `[syntax]` commits; *Growing a Syntax* (FOOL 2009) co-author |
| **Eric Allen** (233) | ea144895, EricAllen | 2007-06 → 2011-07 | Certain — spec co-author, co-PI with Steele |
| **Guy L. Steele Jr.** (177) | gls, Guy Steele | 2008-07 → 2012-06 | Certain |
| **Janus Dam Nielsen** (144) | jdn | 2007-10 → 2009-01 | High — syntax-abstraction commits; *Growing a Syntax* co-author |
| **Scott Kilpatrick** (119) | skilpat | 2008-02 → 2011-08 | **Verified**: spec acknowledgments ("skilpat, who signed SCA"); GitHub github.com/skilpat; OOPSLA 2011 co-author |
| **Tristan King** (112) | tristan.king@gmail.com | 2012-01 → 2012-06 | Real name in history; mailing-list admin "tristan"; compiler tests (BigOpTests, BirdCount). Background unresolved |
| **Michael Spiegel** (110) | mspiegel | 2007-11 → 2008-08 | **Verified**: spec acknowledgments ("mspiegel, who signed SCA"); interpreter/memory-footprint work |
| **Nels Beckman** (95) | nbeckman | 2008-05 → 2009-07 | High — typechecker commits; CMU PhD student era |
| **Victor Luchangco** (76) | victorl, Victor Luchangco | 2008-07 → 2012-05 | Certain — spec co-author |
| **Dan Smith** (64) | ds210953, dlsmith | 2007-05 → 2008-07 | High — ID→username handoff (June 5→8, 2007, both on early type checker); maintained ASTGen and plt.jar, both from Rice's JavaPLT, where Smith was |
| **I-Ting Angelina Lee** (62) | angelee | 2008-05 → 2008-11 | Medium-high — desugarer/closure-conversion for object expressions; MIT intern era |
| **Andrew P. Black?** (56) | black | 2008-08 → 2008-12 | Medium — printing-in-the-presence-of-concurrency library work over one semester, consistent with a Fall 2008 sabbatical visit; unconfirmed |
| **Karl Naden** (48) | karl.naden | 2011-06 → 2012-08 | **Verified**: his CMU page — Oracle Labs intern, summer 2011, "techniques for instantiating generic types at runtime"; his 2012-08-31 instantiation writeup is nearly the last commit of the whole history |
| **Steve Heller** (35) | steve.heller | 2008-08 → 2008-12 | Certain by name; listed in spec acknowledgments; benchmark programs (paraffins, gauntlet) |
| **Jean-Baptiste Tristan** (27) | Jean-Baptiste Tristan | 2011-11 → 2012-01 | Certain — Oracle Labs researcher; experimental component-system prototype and ZZ/NN64 numeric test suites |
| **Ryan Culpepper** (23) | ryanc | 2008-05 → 2008-08 | High — grammar composition / macro keywords; *Growing a Syntax* co-author |
| **Kento Emoto** (6) | emoken | 2008-12 → 2009-07 | High — spec acknowledgments list Emoto (U. Tokyo); commits are "GoGs (generators of generators) for 2D arrays", his research topic |
| **Changhee Park** (8) | changhee.park | 2010-04 → 2012-06 | High — pattern-matching desugarer/typechecker; KAIST, Ryu's group |
| **Claire Alvis** (7) | Claire Alvis | 2012-05 → 2012-07 | Certain by name — deterministic random numbers, contention management; Flood's commits mention "pair programming with calvis" |
| senokay (19) | senokay | 2010-06 → 2010-08 | Unresolved — summer 2010, ReflectiveQuickCheck library (intern-shaped tenure) |
| Crink (26) | Crink | 2008-10 → 2010-04 | Unresolved — editor support (GtkSourceView), library fixes "tested at work"; likely external SCA contributor |
| joeuser (9) | joeuser | 2007-06 → 2007-07 | Unresolved — real ASTGen work under a placeholder account |
| envia (2) | envia | 2010-06-15 | Unresolved — one-day DPLL-in-Fortress contribution |

(Revival-era commits — 2026 — are excluded from the historical record
above.)

## Who wrote what, by subsystem

Top committers per path, `--full-history`, largest first:

| Subsystem | Principal authors |
|---|---|
| **Parser** (`parser/`, `parser_util/`, the four Rats! grammars) | Ryu, overwhelmingly (436 + 200); Chase and Nielsen minor |
| **Syntax abstractions** (extensible syntax/macros) | Ryu, Nielsen, Rafkind, Culpepper — the *Growing a Syntax* team |
| **AST definition** (`Fortress.ast`) | Ryu (248), Chase, Hilburn, Smith |
| **ASTGen tool** | Smith (early), then Chase, Steele |
| **Interpreter** (reference evaluator) | Ryu (424), Chase (221+), Maessen (164), Flood (86) |
| **Native glue** (`glue/`) | Maessen (82), Ryu (76) |
| **Type checker** (Scala, `scala_src/`) | Ryu (176), Hilburn (165), Chase (129), Steele (57), Kilpatrick (39) |
| **Compiler / JVM backend** (`codegen/`) | Chase, dominant (210+123 as two identities); Maessen, Steele |
| **Bytecode optimizer** | Flood, Chase, Steele |
| **Runtime** (work-stealing, transactions, generic instantiation) | Flood, Chase, Steele, Naden |

## What landed

| trait | declaration | body |
|---|---|---|
| `ZZ32` | `widen(self): ZZ64` | `jIntToLong(self)` |
| `ZZ32` | `unsigned(self): NN32` | `jMakeNN32FromZZ32(self)` |
| `ZZ64` | `narrow(self): ZZ32` | `jLongOverflowingToInt(self)` |

One new native binding, `simpleUnsignedIntArith.toLong => jUnsignedIntToLong` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:86`), because the import block had no int-to-long conversion that zero-extends and `NN32.widen` needs one. ## Where this fix belongs

`explorations/coordinator/map/spec-to-implementation.md:323` puts the numeric tower's library side in the prelude column and §4.3 at `:399-410` says what the compiler prelude has of it: nothing above `Number`, and each fixed-size trait carries its own flat declarations. §4.1 at `:356` says the same of operators declared inside a trait — "the compiler prelude declares its own". So a conversion between two fixed-size integer traits is a prelude declaration and a prelude body, not a checker or a codegen change; `explorations/coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md:449` and `:483-484` give the native mechanism it stands on, `import java` plus `nativeHelpers/`, which is what the bodies use.

The four names are functional methods, not getters: `widen(self): ZZ64` is invoked as `widen(x)`, which is the form `ProjectFortress/tests/fib13.fss:30`, `longPrim.fss:23`, `UnsignedTest.fss:17` and `NumberPrintTest.fss:52` all write, and the form the interpreter's api uses for the same four names.

The question asked was "has the team solved this here already, and in how many ways", and the answer is in the file being edited.

**Widening `ZZ32` to `ZZ64`: one way.** `coerce(x: ZZ32) = jIntToLong(x)` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:575`). `widen` uses the same native.

Past the import block, `longOverflowingToInt` is used once — `getter asZZ32(): ZZ32` at `:576` — and `longLowHalfToInt` sixteen times, every one of them a shift count where truncation modulo the word width is the operation. The other five are used nowhere. So the plainly-named signed narrowing in this world already exists and it throws.

**Bit reinterpretation: four getters.** `ZZ64.bitsAsNN64` (`:578`), `ZZ32.bitsAsNN32` (`:663`), `NN32.bitsAsZZ32` (`:753`), `NN64.bitsAsZZ64` (`:819`). `unsigned` and `signed` are the functional-method spellings of exactly these four, and their bodies are the same four native calls.

**Widening `NN32` to `NN64`: one site, and it is wrong.** `jIntToLong(jMakeZZ32FromNN32(...))` appeared once in the whole file, at what is now `:816`, and `jIntToLong` appeared twice in total, there and at `:575`. That is the count rule 2 asks for: one site, repaired here, and no second one. In the landed tree `jIntToLong` is again at two sites, `coerce(x: ZZ32)` at `:575` and the new `ZZ32.widen` at `:745`, and neither has an `NN32` on the other side of it.

The slot was reserved and never filled. As with `jIntToLong` one paragraph above, the count is the pre-edit one and the landed tree differs: `:86` is now called once, by this rung's own `NN64.narrow` at `:874`, and `:94` and `:101` are still called nowhere — `:94` being the native the alternative decision would have used.

Thirteen plainly-named members of those two traits take an Overflowing native; nineteen more do in `trait ZZ32` and `trait ZZ64`. `narrow` is a plain name, so by the file's own convention it takes `longOverflowingToUnsignedInt`.

**No competing declaration.** No `.fss` under `ProjectFortress/tests/` or any `*_tests/` directory declares any of the four; the only other declarations in the tree are the interpreter prelude's own and `ProjectFortress/not_working_static_tests/BuiltinTest.fss:68,72`, which declares its own `widen` and `unsigned` inside its own trait and is not in a gated corpus. The four names are absent from the prose chapters. Saturating addition and subtraction on fixed-size integers are expressed by ⊞ and ⊟. Nothing here rests on that inversion — the decision below rests on the *plain name* taking the Overflowing native, which is a separate count over thirty-two members and is unaffected by which of the two decorated spellings 

**The decision, and it is a decision: `narrow` throws `IntegerOverflow` when the value does not fit, on both the signed and the unsigned side.** Four things argue for it. The file's own convention, counted above: thirty-two plainly-named members of the four numeric traits take an Overflowing native, and the wrapping and saturating spellings take the other two. This world's own signed narrowing, `asZZ32` at `:576`, already throws, so a truncating `narrow` would put two plainly-named signed narrowings with different answers in one trait. The team's own import block reserved all three unsigned narrowings and used none, so the plain slot was left open and the convention says which of the three fills it. And the specification's twice-stated rule that an integer result that does not fit throws `IntegerOverflow`, with truncation given its own spelling elsewhere.

**What the alternative costs, since the alternative has real evidence behind it.** Truncating on the unsigned side is what the interpreter does (`UnsignedLong.java:230-234`) and what `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss:210-211` assert, at the deliberately chosen out-of-range values 2^63 and 2^64-1: `widen(narrow(-x1)) = (x1 LSHIFT 32)-1` and `widen(narrow(x1 LSHIFT 63)) = x0`. The file passes today — measured, `probes/walk-unsignedtest.txt`, `PASS?` and exit 0. So choosing to throw makes those two assertions a walk-against-compiled divergence on the day `UnsignedTest.fss` compiles, and the specification does not settle it because it does not mention `narrow`. That divergence is measured both ways here and carried as provisional ledger row W-2; it is the price of the decision and it is not hidden. # seed-worktree.sh <base-worktree> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
#
# Makes a worktree that is ready to compile and run Fortress without building anything, by copying the
# build and the caches of a baseline worktree that has been built once, and translating the parts of the

component ConvValues
export Executable

kind(v: Any): String =
  typecase v of
    ZZ32 => "ZZ32"
    ZZ64 => "ZZ64"
    NN32 => "NN32"
    NN64 => "NN64"
    ZZ => "ZZ"
    else => "other"
  end

show(label: String, f: () -> Any): () =
  try
    v = f()
    println(label " = " v " : " kind(v))
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => println(label " -> IntegerOverflow")
  end

run() = do
  (* ZZ32 values *)
  zMOne: ZZ32 = -1
  zMin: ZZ32 = -2147483647 - 1
  zMax: ZZ32 = 2147483647
  (* ZZ64 values *)
  lMOne: ZZ64 = widen(zMOne)
  lMin: ZZ64 = -9223372036854775807 - 1
  lMax: ZZ64 = 9223372036854775807
  l2p32p5: ZZ64 = 4294967301
  lBelow: ZZ64 = -2147483649
  (* NN32 values, by unsigned, since walk refuses a numeral at an NN32 binding (row 454) *)
  nAll: NN32 = unsigned(zMOne)
  nHigh: NN32 = unsigned(zMin)
  (* NN64 values *)
  mAll: NN64 = unsigned(lMOne)
  mHalf: NN64 = unsigned(lMin)
  m2p32p5: NN64 = unsigned(l2p32p5)
  (* ZZ values: numerals past ZZ64 are ZZ under walk (P-76) *)
  b2p64p5: ZZ = 18446744073709551621
  bBelow: ZZ = -9223372036854775809
  b2p32p5: ZZ = big(l2p32p5)
  bTop: ZZ = big(lMax)

  println("-- ZZ32")
  show("widen(ZZ32 -1)", fn () => widen(zMOne))
  show("widen(ZZ32 MIN)", fn () => widen(zMin))
  show("unsigned(ZZ32 -1)", fn () => unsigned(zMOne))
  show("unsigned(ZZ32 MIN)", fn () => unsigned(zMin))
  show("narrow(ZZ32 MAX)", fn () => narrow(zMax))
  show("big(ZZ32 MIN)", fn () => big(zMin))
  show("numerator(ZZ32 -1)", fn () => numerator(zMOne))
  println("-- ZZ64")
  show("narrow(ZZ64 2^32+5)", fn () => narrow(l2p32p5))
  show("narrow(ZZ64 -(2^31)-1)", fn () => narrow(lBelow))
  show("narrow(ZZ64 MAX)", fn () => narrow(lMax))
  show("narrow(ZZ64 MIN)", fn () => narrow(lMin))
  show("widen(ZZ64 MAX)", fn () => widen(lMax))
  show("unsigned(ZZ64 -1)", fn () => unsigned(lMOne))
  show("unsigned(ZZ64 MIN)", fn () => unsigned(lMin))
  show("big(ZZ64 MIN)", fn () => big(lMin))
  println("-- NN32")
  show("widen(NN32 2^32-1)", fn () => widen(nAll))
  show("signed(NN32 2^32-1)", fn () => signed(nAll))
  show("signed(NN32 2^31)", fn () => signed(nHigh))
  println("-- NN64")
  show("narrow(NN64 2^64-1)", fn () => narrow(mAll))
  show("narrow(NN64 2^32+5)", fn () => narrow(m2p32p5))
  show("signed(NN64 2^64-1)", fn () => signed(mAll))
  show("signed(NN64 2^63)", fn () => signed(mHalf))
  println("-- ZZ")
  show("narrow(ZZ 2^32+5)", fn () => narrow(b2p32p5))
  show("narrow(ZZ 2^64+5)", fn () => narrow(b2p64p5))
  show("narrow(ZZ -(2^63)-1)", fn () => narrow(bBelow))
  show("widen(ZZ 2^64+5)", fn () => widen(b2p64p5))
  show("widen(ZZ -(2^63)-1)", fn () => widen(bBelow))
  show("widen(ZZ 2^63-1)", fn () => widen(bTop))
  println("-- coercions at a typed binding")
  c1: ZZ64 = nAll
  println("ZZ64 binding of NN32 2^32-1 = " c1 " : " kind(c1))
  c2: NN64 = nAll
  println("NN64 binding of NN32 2^32-1 = " c2 " : " kind(c2))
  c3: ZZ = mAll
  println("ZZ binding of NN64 2^64-1 = " c3 " : " kind(c3))
  c4: ZZ = nAll
  println("ZZ binding of NN32 2^32-1 = " c4 " : " kind(c4))
  c5: ZZ64 = zMin
  println("ZZ64 binding of ZZ32 MIN = " c5 " : " kind(c5))
  c6: ZZ = lMin
  println("ZZ binding of ZZ64 MIN = " c6 " : " kind(c6))
  println("-- the ZZ32 overflow control")
  show("ZZ32 MAX + 1", fn () => zMax + 1)
end
end
EOF

content.content:
Fixed bug in ApiIndexExtractor that was using the .ast of a getter or setter method rather than the .fnDecl for "reporting".
Tightened up the data types in compiler/index so that getters are represented by a Map[Id, FieldGetterMethod] rather than simply a Map[Id,Method], and similarly setters are represented by a Map[Id, FieldSetterMethod] rather than simply a Map[Id,Method].  This required some code changes in StypesUtil, ApiTypeExtractor, CodeGen, and TypeCheckerTestCase, but apparently nowhere else.
Split up GenTest5 into three pieces: part went into ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin, part into new file Library/GeneratorLibrary, and part into ProjectFortress/library_tests/GenTest8.
In SNodeUtil, 10000 was not a high enough limit on freshNameCounter in makeFreshnameHelper.  Changed it to freshNameCounter+10000, so that on each try you get 10000 chances.
In TraitTable.scala, changed two uses of JOption.Some to JOption.wrap (it was wrapping a null pointer).

content.content:
\section{Integers}
\seclabel{basic-integers}

The trait \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\STR{ZZ}) encompasses all finite integers,
the results of starting from \EXP{0} and repeatedly adding or subtracting \EXP{1} a finite number of times.

\Library\ also declare four integer types of fixed size.
The five integer types are these:

\begin{tabbing}
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\STR{ZZ}) is the set of integers (it coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} (\STR{ZZ64}) is the set of integers representable in 64-bit two's-complement form (it coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\STR{ZZ32}) is the set of integers representable in 32-bit two's-complement form.
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64} (\STR{NN64}) is the set of integers representable in 64-bit unsigned binary form (it coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} (\STR{NN32}) is the set of integers representable in 32-bit unsigned binary form.
\end{tabbing}

Like every number type, each of them is a subtype of \TYP{Number} and of no other
number type (\secref{basic-rationals}), and each coerces into \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}.
An integer type coerces from each other integer type all of whose values it holds,
as listed above; every other conversion between integer types is written explicitly.

Among the explicit conversions, the method \VAR{narrow} converts a value of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and a value of
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64} to \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, by keeping its low 32 bits: the result
is the value of the narrower type that is congruent to the argument modulo
\EXP{2^{32}}.
A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other wraps, and no
\TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.

The operators \OPR{LSHIFT} and \OPR{RSHIFT} shift the bits of an integer of any of
the five types by a count of any integer type, and return a value of the type of
the integer shifted.
On \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\VAR{shift}(x,k)} and
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\VAR{shift}(x,-k)}.
On a fixed-size type of width \VAR{n}, for a nonnegative count \VAR{k},
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\lfloor x/2^{k} \rfloor}, and
\EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k} is the value of the type that is congruent to
\EXP{x \cdot 2^{k}} modulo \EXP{2^{n}}: the bits shifted out are lost, and no
\TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.
So a count at or beyond the width gives \EXP{0} for a left shift, and for a right
shift \EXP{0}, or \EXP{-1} if \VAR{x} is negative.
A negative count shifts the other way: \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} (-k)} is
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k}, and \EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} (-k)} is \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k}.
The count is read by its value, whatever its type: an \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} count of
\EXP{2^{63}} or more is beyond the width, not negative.
\revision{revival-shifts}{The Working Draft of February 2011 named neither
\VAR{narrow} nor \OPR{LSHIFT} and \OPR{RSHIFT}, which \library\ declare on the
integer types; the two paragraphs above state the rules the revival decided for
them.}

It is often desirable to know that an integer lies in a subset of its type,
such as the positive values or the nonzero values.
As for the rationals, such subsets are not types of their own:
