(*) Test exceptional behavior of ZZ32 operators that can overflow or wrap or saturate.

shouldOverflow(f: () -> ZZ32): Boolean =
  try
    ignore f()
    false
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => true
    Exception => false 
  end

shouldDivideByZero(f: () -> ZZ32): Boolean =
  try
    ignore f()
    false
  catch e

tests=IntConversionsRungW
link
run

entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

input.prompt: Quote verbatim what the manual says about converting an integer to a narrower integer type: does Int32(x) or convert throw InexactError when the value does not fit, and how does one get truncation (x % Int32, rem)? Also overflow behaviour of arithmetic (wraps). Quote short exact sentences.

toolu_01XYcSPP2X7MR2XB6XNxmffz.prompt: Quote verbatim what the manual says about converting an integer to a narrower integer type: does Int32(x) or convert throw InexactError when the value does not fit, and how does one get truncation (x % Int32, rem)? Also overflow behaviour of arithmetic (wraps). Quote short exact sentences.

content.content:
The documentation says:

> The resulting `Int` value is represented by the least significant 32 bits of this `Long` value.

The page doesn't mention an exception or error, so the value is truncated to its low 32 bits.

```kotlin
println(4_294_967_297L.toInt())  // 1: 2^32 + 1, low 32 bits are 1
println((-2_147_483_649L).toInt()) // 2147483647: wraps to Int.MAX_VALUE
```

The page doesn't say whether `Int32(x)` or `convert` throws `InexactError` when a value doesn't fit. It also doesn't describe truncation with `% Int32` or `rem`. For those details, check the Conversion and Promotion section of the manual or the `Base` documentation.

On overflow, the page says:

> "In Julia, exceeding the maximum representable value of a given type results in a wraparound behavior:"

It gives this example:

```julia
julia> x = typemax(Int64)
9223372036854775807

julia> x + 1
-9223372036854775808
```

It also says that integer arithmetic performs "modular arithmetic". To detect overflow instead of silently wrapping, the page points to the `Base.Checked` module, whose operations "trigger errors if an overflow occurs." For values that must not overflow, it recommends `BigInt`.

content.content:
The page doesn't cover InexactError, values that can't be represented in the target type, or truncating integer conversion with `%` or `rem`. It doesn't mention `%` or `rem` at all.

The closest content is about failed conversions in general. It says:

> "Conversion isn't always possible, in which case a MethodError is thrown"

It also says conversion is usually lossless:

> "It is also usually lossless; converting a value to a different type and back again should result in the exact same value."

input.prompt: Find the docstring for rem(x::Integer, T::Type{<:Integer}) / x % T, and quote it verbatim (it describes truncating conversion, e.g. "Find y::T such that x ≡ y (mod n)..."). Also quote any mention that this differs from convert/T(x) which throws InexactError.

toolu_01TWPSiBQsy8SWjX2R3NWdvQ.prompt: Find the docstring for rem(x::Integer, T::Type{<:Integer}) / x % T, and quote it verbatim (it describes truncating conversion, e.g. "Find y::T such that x ≡ y (mod n)..."). Also quote any mention that this differs from convert/T(x) which throws InexactError.

content.content:
The docstring is listed under `Base.mod`, with the signatures `rem(x::Integer, T::Type{<:Integer})::T`, `mod(x::Integer, T::Type{<:Integer})::T`, and `%(x::Integer, T::Type{<:Integer})::T`. It reads, in part:

> "Find `y::T` such that `x` ≡ `y` (mod n), where n is the number of integers representable in `T`,"

> "If `T` can represent any integer (e.g. `T == BigInt`), then this operation corresponds to a conversion to `T`."

The docstring does not mention `convert`, `T(x)`, or `InexactError`, so there is no quoted statement about how it differs from those. The only `InexactError` mention on the page is in the `round` entry, which is a different function.

The docstring's example shows `129 % Int8` returning `-127` and `129 % BigInt` returning `129`. That is the wrapping behavior for fixed-width types and the identity-like behavior for `BigInt`.

throw_inexacterror(func::Symbol, to, val) = throw(InexactError(func, to, val))

function check_sign_bit(::Type{To}, x) where {To}
    @inline
    # the top bit is the sign bit of x but "sign bit" sounds better in stacktraces
    # n.b. if x is signed, then bitsizeof(x) === bitsizeof(To), otherwise bitsizeof(x) >= bitsizeof(To)
    is_top_bit_set(x) && throw_inexacterror(bitsizeof(x) === bitsizeof(To) ? :convert : :trunc, To, x)
    x
end

function checked_trunc_sint(::Type{To}, x::From) where {To,From}
    @inline
    y = trunc_int(To, x)
    back = sext_int(From, y)
    eq_int(x, back) || throw_inexacterror(:trunc, To, x)
    y
end

function checked_trunc_uint(::Type{To}, x::From) where {To,From}
    @inline
    y = trunc_int(To, x)
    back = zext_int(From, y)
    eq_int(x, back) || throw_inexacterror(:trunc, To, x)
    y
end

content.content:
- P-68 **On the float types, `floor` and `ceiling` return the same float type, while the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ`, the unbounded integer.** So `floor(2.5)` is the `RR64` value 2.0, and ⌊2.5⌋ is to be the `ZZ` value 2. Row 330: one library rung after the switch-over, which first counts the interpreter tests whose output changes, then makes the brackets, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ` in each of the library's declarations of them; today `truncate` is `ZZ64` on both paths, the brackets are `ZZ64` under walk and `RR64` compiled, and `round` is `ZZ64`, but `ZZ` in the `FortressLibrary` component's `trait RR64`.
- P-26 **Where the type group's later positions conflict with the specification's early text, the later positions win.** The early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run, with performance as the goal and specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. Specialization, in the type group's design, is a special version of a generic function for one instantiation, such as `tail(x: List[ZZ])` beside `tail[X](x: List[X])`, which dispatch chooses at run time. Where the two conflict, the specification is revised to follow their later word (P-95 records each change with its reason). Their later word includes the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings in 2009 and 2010 (P-43: the library's numbers are flat in the same way), Karl Naden's 2012 wr
- P-27 **What a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library, in the library's own way.** A program written on this library has a part that states its algorithm, and it can have a part that builds domain-independent machinery that the library lacks, as both microGPT programs do. A form of that second part goes into the standard library when, on reasonable judgment, it is not an extension of the program's own domain; a form that the library has for one number type, rank or sibling trait and lacks for another is the plainest case. Whoever writes it there first studies how the library does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern, such as its `excludes` clauses. This rule governs how the library is extended; it does not choose between two of the team's designs of the language (P-26).
- F-132 **Under `walk`, fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` when the result does not fit, as the specification says.** It builds P-73. Every arithmetic operation on a fixed width whose result can leave its type raises it, `^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM` included, and a program can catch it. Three kinds of operation raise nothing: the wrapping operators (F-130) and `narrow`, the written conversion of a `ZZ64` to `ZZ32` or an `NN64` to `NN32` (P-72), which keep the low bits; and the shifts `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT`, which lose the bits shifted out (F-125). Gated by `tests/FixedWidthOverflowRungB.fss` (`+`, `-`, `DOT` (`·`), `DIV`, negation and absolute value, on the four fixed widths) and `tests/PowChooseLcmRungE.fss` (`^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM`). The compiled path is outside this fact. Its known gaps: the compiler prelude's ranges raise `IntegerOverflow` where their bounds sum beyon
- F-124 **On the compiled path, at or beyond the width of `ZZ32` or `ZZ64`, `LSHIFT` gives 0 and `RSHIFT` the sign; both reverse on a negative count, and `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits.** "The sign" is 0 for a nonnegative value and -1 for a negative one. `ZZ64`'s and `NN64`'s `narrow` to 32 bits keeps the low 32 bits. `<<`, `>>` and `<<<` keep their own rules, and `asZZ32` throws out of range. Negation, absolute value and division overflow only at the minimum value and test exactly for it, so the minimum raises `IntegerOverflow`, and `|0|`, `-0` and `0 DIV -1` answer 0. Addition and subtraction test the sign bits, and multiplication computes the exact product (`Math.multiplyExact` on `ZZ64`, a range-checked 64-bit product on `ZZ32`). So these raise `IntegerOverflow` on every overflow, and a zero factor answers 0. `ZZ`'s `<<<` raises a catchable `IntegerOverflow` on a shift that it cannot
- F-172 **The specification's integer chapter states the library's integer rules.** `narrow` converts a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` to `ZZ32`, and an `NN64` to `NN32`, by keeping the low 32 bits; a value that does not fit wraps, and nothing is thrown. `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` work on the five integer types. On `ZZ` they are `shift`, which is exact at any count. On a fixed-size type, `LSHIFT` loses the bits shifted out and throws nothing. `GCD` and `LCM` are nonnegative, and one that a fixed-size type cannot hold throws `IntegerOverflow`. At a negative power, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 throws `DivisionByZero`, and any other base throws `IntegerOverflow`. The library follows the same power rule under walk; the compiled path's own library does not (F-263). # What the code that relies on wrapping should become
20:2. **The named truncating conversion** (means to wrap). `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits of a `ZZ64` on both paths, decided by Pavol for row 346 (`POSITIONS.md:76`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Long.java:248-252` is `(int) x`; the compiled body `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:659`). So `narrow(widen(c1) widen(n) + widen(c2))` is an exact 32-bit wrap with no overflow anywhere. `ZZ`'s `narrow` and `widen` (to `ZZ32` and to `ZZ64`) also keep the low bits under `walk`, `BigInteger.intValue` and `longValue` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:891-895`; 
22:4. **Bit operators in place of arithmetic** (either need). `BITAND`, `BITOR`, `BITXOR` and `BITNOT` never overflow, and shifts let the bits shifted out fall off silently on both paths, by Pavol's decision on row 335 (`POSITIONS.md:73`). So "the bits below position `b`" can be written `BITNOT (widen(-1) LSHIFT b)`, which touches no arithmetic operator, instead of `(widen(1) LSHIFT b) - 1`.
31:10. **The binary-word layer's methods** (either need). The specification's lowest layer, `BinaryWord`, from which it says types such as `ZZ64` are to be "defined by libraries coded entirely in Fortress" (`Specification/advanced-lib/binary.tex:14-34`), spells every variant as a method: `wrappingAdd`, `wrappingSubtract`, `wrappingNegate`; `add(other, carryIn): (T, Bit)`, which returns the carry bit beside the sum; `signedAdd(other, overflowAction: () -> T)`, where the caller supplies what happens on overflow; `saturatingSignedAdd`; `multiplyLow`, `multiplyHigh` and `multiplyDouble`, the full 
40:- **The unsigned types.** The specification's overflow rule covers every integer result (`opr-overview.tex:155`), so `NN32` and `NN64` do not wrap by design. Under `walk` they wrap today: their natives call `com.naturalbridge.misc.Unsigned.add`, which is a bare `iadd` (read with `javap` from `ProjectFortress/third_party/unsigned/unsigned.jar`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/NN32.java:109-112`). Row 379 does not cover them (section 11).
73:- Route A (`POSITIONS.md:92`) flattens the tower into siblings, each with its own algebra, a wider type converting from a narrower one. Each fixed width is then its own ring under ∔, ∸ and ⨰: the integers modulo 2^32 and modulo 2^64 are different rings, and a `ZZ32` ∔ `ZZ64` converts to `ZZ64` first and wraps at 64 bits.
81:- Where the designers already departed from Java, on record: `+` checked where Java wraps (Steele's Overflowing natives, 2011; row 379 for `walk`); round half to even (row 329); nonnegative `GCD` (row 334); the smart shift (row 335). The one integer decision that followed Java is `narrow`, which truncates as a Java cast does (row 346), and that is a conversion with its own name, not an arithmetic operator.
96:- **C.** Signed overflow is undefined behaviour and unsigned arithmetic is reduced modulo 2^n (C11 § 6.5 ¶ 5, § 6.2.5 ¶ 9; not fetched).
133:- Outside the eleven: `UnsignedTest`'s use of unary `-` on an unsigned value as 2^w minus a number, `dc41d5000`, 2008-07-21, Steele (section 11).
156:- **(d) `LinearCongruential`**, `Library/Random.fss:235` (measured) and `:241` (by reading). It means arithmetic modulo 2^48, done through arithmetic modulo 2^64. It becomes `((mult DOTTIMES widen(state)) DOTPLUS add) MOD modulus`: the same values, no cost, `MOD` bringing a negative wrapped value back into range as it does today. This is right only because 2^48 divides 2^64. The object is generic in its modulus (`Random.fss:222`) and built once, with 2^48 (`:253`); for a modulus that is not a power of two, today's code and this one both give wrong numbers without a word (section 11). Alter
157:- **(e) `ChunkedSparseArray.secondaryIndex`**, `Library/ChunkedSparseArray.fss:76` (measured). It means the bits below the mask. It becomes `popCount((mask DOTMINUS 1) BITAND fe)`. Alternatives: `if mask < 0 then BITNOT mask else mask - 1 end`, or, from the bit index `indexAndMask` already computes (`:75`), `BITNOT (widen(-1) LSHIFT b)` (way 4).
159:- **(g) `HeapTest`'s `spread`**, `ProjectFortress/tests/HeapTest.fss:95-99`. It means a scramble modulo 2^32: with `c1` odd, `n ↦ c1 n + c2` maps `ZZ32` onto itself one to one, so the test's keys stay distinct. It becomes `((c1 DOTTIMES n) DOTPLUS c2, n)`. Alternative: `narrow(widen(c1) widen(n) + widen(c2))` (way 2), which never overflows and gives the same value.
160:- **(h) `intPrim.fss:21-22` and `longPrim.fss:21-22`.** They assert of `+` and `-` exactly what the specification refuses; their author's intent (section 8) was "the boundary behaves as it should". 174:**Option 2, restructure everything and declare no operator.** Every site is rewritten in the library's avoid-overflow habits: the zero case in the split, a highest-set-bit primitive or a guard for the `+1`, masks by shift, a sign case in `IntMap`, the hash through `widen` and `narrow`, the generator exact through `ZZ` or by split multiplication, and the tests asserting the throw, with the properties restated on the range where `+` answers.
